newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Romania PM says economy in crisis, seeks investment.
newsitem.headline: Romania PM says economy in crisis, seeks investment.

text.p: Visiting Romanian Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea said on Thursday his country's economy was in crisis and urged Hungarians to invest in Romania as relations improve after years of strain.
Ciorbea, on his first state visit abroad since his centre-right coalition took power from leftists last year, said he had inherited an economy in a "sorry state".
"We must quickly privatise state-owned industries within a year from now," Ciorbea told a breakfast meeting attended by about 100 Hungarian businessmen.

"We will not be able to overcome the economic crisis without foreign investment," he added on the second day of his two-day visit, which includes a trip to the "economic miracle" town of Szekesfehervar, home to subsidiaries of several multi-national corporations.

Romania, with 22 million people, is East Europe's second largest market after Poland but investment has lagged in the post-communist era and is barely one tenth of the $15 billion of direct foreign investment in Hungary.

Ciorbea, who pointedly chose Hungary for his first official trip to signal a thaw in relations previously strained by concern over Romania's 1.6 million ethnic Hungarians, said he saw a big role for Hungarian business in Romania.
"We are waiting for you to bring your experience and your capital to the Romanian market," he said. "We are eagerly waiting for you to join in the privatisation of the Romanian economy."
Ciorbea is accompanied by key economic ministers who signed agreements on Wednesday to develop ties in the economic, transport and foreign policy fields.

Another main theme of his visit has been linking Romanian and Hungarian efforts to join NATO in the first round of expansion of the western military alliance, to be decided at a summit in Madrid in July.

Horn, whose country is considered a front-runner for first-round NATO expansion, said on Wednesday it was in Hungary's "strategic interest" that Romania, whose chances are deemed less sure, should also join.

Horn paid tribute to Ciorbea, who for the first time has appointed ethnic Hungarians as government ministers and has supported the use of bilingual signs and of minority languages in public administration and courts.
Previous Romanian governments have made promises, Horn said, "but with this one there is real hope of the promises coming through".
